generated_frontmatter.abstract: Wind-power forecasting during meteorological extremes combines limited target labels with source--target distribution differences. We formulate the Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR) using symmetric centered source-residual variance, a projected predictive-mean discrepancy, and weighted pinball loss. A frozen chronological comparison uses 128 target fitting labels and separates six primary within-site tasks from six secondary leave-one-farm-out stress tasks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 18.090\%, ranked 3rd of six, and was outside the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 17.694\%, ranked 5th of six, and remained in the conservative first tier. First-tier membership is non-rejection of inferiority rather than equivalence or superiority. Of 60 Holm-adjusted task comparisons, 1 favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator. With its settings held fixed, TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four in the primary matched scope and 2nd of four in the secondary matched scope; 2 Holm-adjusted removal effects favored TL-QLDMR and 0 favored a removal variant. Its mean-rank positions were 1st and 1st, respectively. The matched effects are conditional because the variants were not independently retuned. The public Q3--Q4 period had been examined previously, so these results are test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation and do not establish universal model superiority.

generated_frontmatter.conclusion: The implementation passes deterministic objective, gradient, and primal--dual consistency checks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting had the lowest observed site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties; it ranked 3rd of six and was excluded from the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, histogram gradient boosting had the lowest observed site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties; it ranked 5th of six and was retained in the conservative first tier. The first-tier statements are non-rejections of inferiority to each empirical endpoint winner and do not establish equivalence, equal performance, or superiority. Among 60 predeclared task-level comparisons, 1 Holm-adjusted finding favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator; non-rejection for the remaining comparisons does not establish equal performance. In the conditional matched-removal analysis for the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR recorded 18.090\% and ranked 2nd of four by macro RMSE, with the lowest mean task rank (2.00); the lowest observed matched endpoint was the no-variance variant at 17.870\%. In the conditional matched-removal analysis for the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR recorded 17.694\% and ranked 2nd of four by macro RMSE, with the lowest mean task rank (2.17); the lowest observed matched endpoint was the no-variance variant at 17.671\%. The separate Farm~6 nine-quantile and earlier calibration studies remain legacy exploratory sensitivity analyses and are not part of the formal evidence chain. Taken together, the formal results provide a scope- and task-dependent assessment of TL-QLDMR rather than evidence of universal superiority. Because the public Q3--Q4 test period had been examined before the frozen protocol was designed, the comparison is test-locked evidence on a reused period and does not provide independent external confirmation.
